source: Stanford Encyclopedia: Folk Psychology as Mental Simulation (entry text, sections 1-6)
finding: Defines the two camps. Simulation theory (ST): we represent others' minds by running our own mind offline, so mindreading is process-driven and information-poor. Theory-theory (TT): we use a tacit folk theory, so it is information-rich and theory-driven.
numbers: Goldman 1989 and 2006 (Simulating Minds) vs Gopnik & Wellman 1992 and Perner & Howes 1992.
limits: Entry text read in two passes; the middle of the entry was not read. Page gives few numbers.
agent_relevance: Background only. TT maps to explicit rule or knowledge prompts; ST maps to role-taking prompts (run the model as the other agent).
quote: ST: mindreading is 'informationally poor and process driven' (Goldman 1989).

source: SEP entry: founders and their positions
finding: Gordon (1986) defends radical simulationism with 'ascent routines': to ask whether X believes p, ask whether p. Heal (1986, Replication and Functionalism) co-founded ST and later (2003) a hybrid: simulate rational transitions, theorize causal ones. Goldman proposes a three-stage model (simulate, introspect, judge) and separates high-level (imagination) from low-level (mirroring) simulation.
limits: Carruthers' scope problem: ascent routines seem to work only for belief, not goals or fear.
agent_relevance: A simulating agent needs the other's inputs (what they know) and then reuses its own reasoning. This is the two-step shape of the SimToM prompt (see a16).

source: SEP entry: objections to simulation
finding: Main objections: Dennett's collapse argument (simulation needs theory about the target, so ST collapses into TT); anti-constitution arguments (judging 'X believes p' is not given by simulating); the mechanism problem (Heal 1994); mirror-neuron evidence is correlational and human action-understanding evidence is 'inconclusive at best' (Hickok 2009).
numbers: Dennett 1987; Fuller 1995; Heal 1994, 1995; Jackson 1999; Gallagher 2007; Spaulding 2012; Hickok 2009.
limits: Entry is a philosopher's summary, not an empirical test.
agent_relevance: For an LLM the objections invert: the model has no separate own mind to reuse; it reuses the same next-token machinery for every role, so simulation and theory are not separable by architecture.

source: SEP entry: egocentric error and the curse of knowledge
finding: ST predicts and explains egocentric errors: we fail to quarantine our own knowledge when simulating someone else (Goldman 2006; Birch & Bloom 2007 curse of knowledge). Critics (Saxe 2005; de Vignemont & Mercier 2016) dispute that this favours ST.
numbers: Goldman 2006; Gordon 1995; Birch & Bloom 2007.
limits: Errors fit ST but also fit TT plus a processing bias.
agent_relevance: LLM agents show the same leak: story facts the character does not know contaminate the answer. A quarantine step (filter context to what the character knows) is the fix, which is what SimToM does.

source: SEP entry: developmental findings and the infant puzzle
finding: Verbal false-belief task (Wimmer & Perner 1983): 3-year-olds usually fail, 4-year-olds usually pass (Wellman et al. 2001 meta-analysis). Nonverbal looking-time tasks show sensitivity at 15 months (Onishi & Baillargeon 2005) and possibly 7 months (Baillargeon et al. 2016). Goldman & Jordan (2013) say ST explains the gap: infants imagine the scene from the other's view (primitive), while the verbal task needs full mindreading plus inhibitory control.
numbers: Ages: fail at 3, pass at 4 (verbal); 15 months (nonverbal looking); 7 months (claimed).
limits: Whether infant success shows belief representation is disputed (Perner & Ruffman 2005; Apperly & Butterfill 2009).
agent_relevance: Separate tracking what someone has seen (cheap, early) from representing a belief that conflicts with reality (costly, needs inhibition). Our agent can implement the first as a filter and the second as an explicit check.

source: Wikipedia: Theory-theory
finding: Page is thin. It says developmental psychologists began advocating the theory theory in the mid-1980s, with Gopnik the main name, and treats simulation as an alternative. It gives no sample sizes or effects.
numbers: No figures.
limits: Low quality as a source; used only to confirm the subfield framing. Does not name Wimmer & Perner, Baron-Cohen or Wellman.
agent_relevance: Background only, as the subfield row says.

source: Wikipedia: Simulation theory of empathy
finding: Lists mirror-neuron and imaging evidence cited for ST and the main counter-evidence. Singer et al. (2004) found pain empathy used affective regions (anterior insula, anterior cingulate) but not sensory pain regions when only a cue was shown, which limits a pure mirroring account. Wicker et al. (2003): anterior insula active both for smelling disgust and watching disgusted faces.
numbers: Harrison et al. 2006: pupils enlarged to 180% made sad faces rated less negative.
limits: Secondary source; content was summarised by a fetch tool, not read in full.
agent_relevance: Shared-substrate evidence supports low-level simulation of feelings. No direct analogue for a text-only agent.

source: Onishi & Baillargeon (2005) Do 15-month-old infants understand false beliefs? Science
finding: Violation-of-expectation task. 15-month-olds watched an actor search for a toy hidden in one of two boxes and looked longer at events that did not fit her true or false belief. The authors concluded infants attribute false beliefs. This broke the older claim that belief understanding appears only at about 4.
numbers: Abstract only (full text server error). Per-condition looking times not recorded.
limits: Only the abstract was read via Europe PMC. Numbers not verified. Later contested (see a09, a10).
agent_relevance: The founding nonverbal paradigm that LLM false-belief tests descend from.
quote: Abstract: 'from a young age, children appeal to mental states--goals, perceptions, and beliefs--to explain the behavior of others.'

source: Kampis, Karman, Csibra, Southgate & Hernik (2021) Two-lab direct replication of Southgate, Senju & Csibra (2007). R Soc Open Sci
finding: Preregistered direct replication with 160 infants aged 24-26 months in Copenhagen and Budapest, original stimuli. No evidence of belief-based action anticipation, and not even reliable anticipation in the control trial.
numbers: 160 tested; 70 excluded; 90 analysed. 49 of 90 (54%) anticipated correctly in familiarization trial 2 (original: 20 of 31, 65%). Of the 49, 22 anticipated correctly at test, p = 0.568, exact binomial (about 45%). Mean looking score 0.47, 95% CI [0.36, 0.57], t(47) = -0.63, p = 0.532.
limits: Only the anticipatory-looking paradigm is undermined. The authors say this does not show infants lack ToM. Original N was 20 (10 per condition).
agent_relevance: Warning for any benchmark built on one paradigm: a headline result can fail replication. Do not rely on one test of belief tracking.
quote: 'we conclude that this paradigm and stimuli do not reliably elicit action anticipation.'

source: Poulin-Dubois & Yott (2018) Probing the depth of infants' theory of mind: disunity in performance across paradigms. Dev Sci
finding: Gave the same infants several ToM paradigms. Performance did not agree across tasks, which suggests infant ToM is not one unified competence.
numbers: Not recorded; full text could not be opened (bot check and Europe PMC error).
limits: Found only as a title in a search result. Treat the claim as unverified until opened.
agent_relevance: Supports splitting theory of mind into separate checks rather than one score.

source: Strachan et al. (2024) Testing theory of mind in large language models and humans. Nature Human Behaviour
finding: Battery of false belief, irony, faux pas, hinting and strange stories given to GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and LLaMA2-70B (15 chats each) against 1,907 humans overall. GPT-4 at or above human on indirect requests, false belief and misdirection; weak on faux pas.
numbers: Human samples per test about 48-51 in the main run. Irony: GPT-4 above humans (P = 0.040, r = 0.32). Faux pas: GPT-4 below humans (P = 5.42e-5, r = 0.55). Humans and LLMs at ceiling on the standard false-belief test. On perturbed variants (transparent containers, asking about the mover) humans (N = 757) also failed on half.
limits: Perturbation fails humans too, so Ullman-style perturbations are not a clean test of ToM. Item content and test type matter.
agent_relevance: Control for a human baseline before calling a perturbation failure a model failure. Model hedging (refusing to commit) can look like missing ToM.
quote: GPT's faux pas failure 'originated from a hyperconservative approach towards committing to conclusions rather than from a genuine failure of inference.'

source: Kosinski (2024) Evaluating large language models in theory of mind tasks. PNAS 121(45):e2405460121
finding: 40 bespoke false-belief tasks (20 unexpected-contents, 20 unexpected-transfer), each with a false-belief scenario, 3 true-belief controls and reversed versions: 16 prompts per task, all must be right. Eleven LLMs tested.
numbers: GPT-3-davinci-002: 5% (CI 0-10). GPT-3-davinci-003 and ChatGPT-3.5-turbo: 20% (CI 11-29), below 3-year-old children. ChatGPT-4: 75% (CI 66-84), compared with 6-year-olds. GPT-4: 90% on contents vs 60% on transfer (chi2 = 8.07, P = 0.01). Davinci-003 fell from 90% to 60% after item fixes and to 20% after adding true-belief controls; GPT-4 fell 95% to 75%. Children benchmark: Wellman et al. meta-analysis of 178 studies.
limits: Preprint (Feb 2023) numbers were much higher; reviewers' controls cut them. Children comparison is across different tasks. GPT-4 still failed at least one prompt in 25% of tasks; older models in 80%.
agent_relevance: Strict scoring (all controls) matters: lenient scoring inflates ToM. Use control items in any agent eval.
quote: GPT-4 'solved 75% of the tasks, matching the performance of 6-y-old children observed in past studies.'

source: Ullman (2023) Large language models fail on trivial alterations to theory-of-mind tasks. arXiv:2302.08399
finding: Small changes that keep the ToM logic (transparent container, protagonist can read the label, an extra move by a second person that restores the object) flip GPT-3.5 answers. Argues for a sceptical null hypothesis: outlying failures outweigh average success.
numbers: Original (from Kosinski preprint): P(popcorn)=100% for contents, P(chocolate)=99% for belief. In several altered scenarios the model still gave the standard false-belief answer with high confidence (reported P values for the label-based belief of about 87-98%, and P(basket) of 74-99% in transfer variants), though a person with the altered facts would answer differently. Scenario-to-number mapping not checked. A handful of anecdotal cases, no sample.
limits: Anecdotal, few items, GPT-3.5 only; probabilities read from the paper text, scenario mapping approximate. Strachan 2024 shows humans also fail half of such perturbations.
agent_relevance: Argues for adversarial variants of every belief test used on the agent.
quote: 'the zero-hypothesis for model evaluation in intuitive psychology should be skeptical'

source: Shapira et al. (2023) Clever Hans or Neural Theory of Mind? Stress testing social reasoning in LLMs. arXiv:2305.14763
finding: Six tasks and an adversarial false-belief set. GPT-4 is strong on original false-belief items but collapses on adversarial variants.
numbers: GPT-4 97% on original unexpected-transfer false-belief items. Other-person variant fell from 93.8% (davinci-002) to 68.8% (GPT-4). Transparent access fell from 66.7% to 0%; 'inon' variant from 71.4% to 0%. FauxPas-EAI 27% for GPT-4.
limits: Newer models can get worse on adversarial items; read from text and figure captions, not per-model tables.
agent_relevance: Reinforces that a belief-tracking claim needs adversarial variants, not just the textbook case.

source: Sap, Le Bras, Fried & Choi (2022) Neural Theory-of-Mind? On the limits of social intelligence in large LMs. arXiv:2210.13312
finding: Early test: GPT-3 lacks social intelligence out of the box on SocialIQa and ToMi.
numbers: GPT-3 55% on SocialIQa and 60% peak on ToMi mental-state questions, both over 30% below humans. Adding up to 35 in-context examples gave about a 1% gain. Later models on multiple choice: GPT-3.5-RLHF 60%, then 67%, and the best at 79.3%, within 10% of humans.
limits: Numbers are for 2022 and 2023 models; later models are higher.
agent_relevance: Baseline for the trend; instruction tuning and RLHF did most of the work, not prompt format.

source: Wilf, Lee, Liang & Morency (2023) Think Twice: perspective-taking improves LLM theory of mind (SimToM). arXiv:2311.10227
finding: The one direct use of simulation theory as a prompt design. Step 1: filter the story to what the character knows (perspective-taking). Step 2: answer the question from that filtered text only. No training.
numbers: False-belief accuracy, BigToM / ToMI: GPT-3.5 0-shot 41.0 / 67.25, CoT 56.25 / 34.0, SimToM 70.5 / 81.0 (+29.5 over 0-shot and +14.2 over CoT on BigToM; +47 over CoT on ToMI). Llama2-7b-chat BigToM FB 47.5 to 70.5. GPT-4 0-shot BigToM FB 89.0; SimToM about the same or slightly lower (BigToM was generated by GPT-4). Oracle perspective-taking: ToMI FB 81.0 to 96, BigToM FB 70.5 to 96. Single-prompt ablation lost much of the gain (BigToM total fell to 58.25%).
limits: PDF table extraction was garbled; GPT-3.5 values were matched using the text's own deltas. Two benchmarks only. The filter step is model-written so errors propagate.
agent_relevance: Directly useful: a two-call role-taking step with an information filter. Keep the filter as its own call (single-prompt ablation lost the effect). The oracle result says filter quality is the bottleneck.
quote: SimToM: 'filtering the context only to what the character in question knows.'

source: Jin et al. (2024) MMToM-QA: multimodal theory of mind question answering (BIP-ALM). arXiv:2401.08743
finding: A theory-based model beats LLMs. BIP-ALM does Bayesian inverse planning (a formal TT model) with language models supplying likelihoods. Benchmark has 600 questions on goals and beliefs in household scenes.
numbers: Multimodal overall: humans 93.0%; GPT-4V 44.0%; BIP-ALM with LLaMA 2 76.7%, with GPT-J 75.3%. Text only: human 82.5%; GPT-4 48.0%; GPT-3.5 38.3%; SimToM w/ GPT-4 52.5%; SymbolicToM w/ GPT-4 63.0%; BIP-ALM about 71%. GPT-4 true-belief type 1.1: 97%, false-belief type 1.2: 12%. GPT-4V video-only 46.0%.
limits: Table columns are easy to mix up; overall column taken as the last. Bayesian inverse planning needs structured symbolic input.
agent_relevance: A hybrid of formal inverse planning with an LLM scoring step beats prompting alone on goal and belief inference. SimToM-style filtering helped little here (48.0 to 52.5).

source: Gandhi, Franken, Gerstenberg & Goodman (2023) Understanding social reasoning in language models with language models (BigToM). NeurIPS
finding: Procedurally generated benchmark from causal templates: 25 controls and 5,000 model-written items covering forward belief, forward action and backward belief inference. GPT-4 patterns match humans but are less reliable.
numbers: GPT-4 forward action false-belief 0-shot .81 without initial belief, .98 with 1-shot (1.00 with 1-shot CoT). Backward belief hardest: humans 82% true-belief and 72% false-belief; GPT-4 0-shot .53 false-belief. Many models score below chance, meaning they reliably attribute the wrong belief. Expert agreement on items 93.94%.
limits: Items written by GPT-4 (possible bias toward GPT-4). False-belief success counted only if the true-belief version also passed.
agent_relevance: Models anchor on an explicitly stated initial belief; backward inference from an action is weakest, which matches agent tasks (inferring what a user wants from what they did).
quote: 'GPT4 has ToM capabilities that mirror human inference patterns, though less reliable, while other LLMs struggle.'

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANToM: a benchmark for stress-testing machine theory of mind in interactions. arXiv:2310.15421
finding: Conversations with information asymmetry. Six question types about the same hidden-information fact test for illusory ToM. Models pass single questions but not the full set.
numbers: Short-context ALL scores: human 87.5%; GPT-4 0613 + CoT 26.6% (June) and 14.8% (Oct); ChatGPT 3.7%; Llama-2-chat 0.4%. Answerability and info-access sets: human 90.6; GPT-4 CoT 40.2 and 57.7 (June). Overall models trail humans by over 70 points on average on the full set.
limits: Fine-tuned Flan-T5 XL reached 53.7 on ALL, still below humans. CoT helped but did not close the gap.
agent_relevance: Use consistency across question types about the same hidden fact as the ToM check, not a single question.

source: Rabinowitz et al. (2018) Machine theory of mind (ToMnet). ICML. arXiv:1802.07740
finding: A meta-learned network that models agents from behaviour alone, in line with Gopnik & Wellman's idea that we use high-level models rather than simulate. It passes a gridworld Sally-Anne test: it predicts an agent's policy changes when a swap is within view and not when outside.
numbers: Swap events had probability 0.1 when the agent stepped on the subgoal. ToMnet predicted corrective behaviour only for in-view swaps, but its visibility boundary was softer than the true agent's. Learned this even when it never saw swap events in training.
limits: Simple gridworlds, trained agents, no human data.
agent_relevance: A learned observer model picks up what could they see without being told, which supports an explicit visibility field in our agent state.

source: van Duijn et al. (2023) Theory of mind in LLMs: 11 models vs children aged 7-10 on advanced tests. arXiv:2310.20320
finding: Tested 11 base and instruction-tuned LLMs and children on false belief, non-literal language and recursive intentionality with rewritten items. Instruction-tuned GPT models beat other models and often children; base models mostly fail even with special prompts.
numbers: Children: 37 aged 7-8 and 36 aged 9-10. Per-model scores not extracted.
limits: Abstract, introduction and method read; results tables not. Numbers are partial.
agent_relevance: Suggests instruction tuning (rewarding cooperative communication) is what adds ToM-like behaviour, not scale alone.

source: Zhu, Zhang & Wang (2024) Language models represent beliefs of self and others. ICML. arXiv:2402.18496
finding: Belief status of different agents can be linearly decoded from hidden activations, and steering along these directions changes ToM task performance. Fits a view with separate self and other belief representations.
numbers: No numbers extracted; intervention-strength sweeps on Mistral-7B are in figures.
limits: Abstract and intervention section skimmed only. Decoding is correlational; small open models.
agent_relevance: Gives internal evidence that role-taking is a distinct operation in the model, which weakly supports a separate role-taking step.

source: Baron-Cohen, Leslie & Frith (1985) Does the autistic child have a theory of mind? Cognition 21:37-46
finding: Sally-Anne test: autistic children mostly failed to predict where Sally would look, while most children with Down syndrome and typical 4-year-olds passed. Used to argue for a specific theory-of-mind deficit, a core result for the theory-module account.
numbers: From memory, not opened: 61 children; about 80% of autistic children failed; about 85% of typical and Down syndrome children passed.
limits: Not opened; numbers recalled and unverified. Small sample; later work found autistic people who pass.
agent_relevance: Background. The test is the template for every LLM false-belief item.

source: Wimmer & Perner (1983) Beliefs about beliefs. Cognition 13:103-128
finding: Original false-belief (unexpected transfer) task with Maxi and the chocolate. Younger children (about 3-4) mostly named the true location; success rose with age to about 6. Founding result for the claim that the child's theory of mind changes at about 4.
numbers: Not opened; exact percentages not recalled with confidence.
limits: Not opened. Cited as the source in Kosinski (a12) and SEP (a05).
agent_relevance: Template for LLM item design.

source: Wellman, Cross & Watson (2001) Meta-analysis of theory-of-mind development: the truth about false belief. Child Dev 72:655-684
finding: Meta-analysis of 178 studies. Children under about 3 fail standard false-belief tasks and performance rises across ages 3 to 5 across task variants. Used as the human norm in Kosinski (a12).
numbers: 178 studies per Kosinski (a12, opened). Per-age proportions not read.
limits: Not opened; only the study count was confirmed through a12 and the SEP.
agent_relevance: Human benchmark for LLM comparisons; the age pattern is robust across task variants.

source: Gallese & Goldman (1998) Mirror neurons and the simulation theory of mind-reading. Trends Cogn Sci 2:493-501
finding: Proposed that macaque F5 mirror neurons are a low-level neural substrate of simulation; the bridge between ST and neuroscience (cited by Wilf et al., a16).
numbers: No numbers read. Mirror neurons found by Rizzolatti and colleagues in macaque premotor area F5 (via SEP, a03).
limits: Not opened. SEP and Wikipedia note the evidence is correlational and concerns actions, not beliefs.
agent_relevance: No direct use for a text agent.

source: Gopnik & Wellman (1992) Why the child's theory of mind really is a theory. Mind & Language 7:145-171
finding: Founding paper of developmental theory-theory: children build a causal-explanatory theory of mind and revise it as evidence accumulates, so errors reflect a wrong theory, not missing simulation. Rabinowitz (a20) cites it for social reasoning using high-level models.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; role described via SEP (a05) and Rabinowitz (a20).
agent_relevance: The theory view supports a revisable store of explicit rules about the other agent.

source: Hybrid accounts: Heal (2003), Perner & Kuhberger (2005) (as reported in SEP)
finding: Both camps converged on hybrids. SEP: Heal simulates rational transitions and theorizes causal ones; Perner later defended a hybrid; the conclusion says a combined ST and TT account is likely, but its form is unclear.
numbers: No empirical numbers.
limits: Only the SEP description was read. Nichols & Stich 2003 not opened.
agent_relevance: Design lesson: do both. Use explicit rules for facts about the world and role-taking for what someone would conclude.

source: Baker, Jara-Ettinger, Saxe & Tenenbaum (2017) Rational quantitative attribution of beliefs, desires and percepts. Nature Human Behaviour 1:0064
finding: Bayesian theory of mind: infer beliefs and desires by inverting a model of a rational planner. Formally a theory-theory with generative planning inside it, so it blurs ST and TT. Cited in Gandhi (a18) and Rabinowitz (a20).
numbers: Not opened; no figures recorded.
limits: Not opened; described only from citing papers.
agent_relevance: Basis of BIP-ALM (a17). Inverse planning is the formal version of what a rational agent would do given what they know.
